newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH's Arnault seen set to get his way on drinks merger.
newsitem.headline: LVMH's Arnault seen set to get his way on drinks merger.

text.p: LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault looks set to derail one of the biggest mergers in British corporate history and oblige Guinness and Grand Metropolitan to swallow his plan for a three-way drinks merger, analysts said on Tuesday.

Industry sources said he was preparing a final offensive this week and was waiting for the go-ahead from Britain's Takeover Panel to present details to investors on the proposed drinks merger that he broadly outlined earlier this month.
"This authorisation could be given today," an industry source said.

Analysts say Arnault, the world's leading luxury magnate and one of France's shrewdest businessmen, looks likely to succeed in thwarting the planned 24 billion pound ($40.2 billion) GrandMet-Guinness merger announced in May.
"I'm pretty sure his plan will go through," one analyst said.
The heads of GrandMet and Guinness said this month they would consider Arnault's plan if it created more shareholder value.
Analysts say the British groups' decision may come as early as Wednesday, when Guinness's board is scheduled to meet. LVMH announced on Monday that Arnault had quit the board.

The group declined to confirm reports that Arnault was travelling to England, possibly on Thursday, to try to convince British holders of Guinness's and GrandMet's dispersed capital that his plan would generate more value than the creation of a sprawling drinks, beer, canned goods and fast foods conglomerate.

Arnault has said he wants to set up an independent, listed company with more than 60 billion francs ($9.9 billion) in sales and a portfolio ranging from Hennessy cognacs and Moet Chandon champagnes to GrandMet's Smirnoff, Gilbey's, J&B and Bailey's brands and Guinness's Johnnie Walker, Dewar's, Gordon and Tanqueray drinks.

Arnault proposes to put LVMH's 66 percent stake in Moet Hennessy, its 14.2 percent stake in Guinness and newly acquired 6.4 percent holding in GrandMet into the new drinks company whose market capitalisation is estimated at roughly 70 billion francs.
Traders reported on Thursday that LVMH, the biggest investor in both Guinness and GrandMet, was shifting its holdings between them in a tactic whose objective was not immediately clear.
